problem.text: A function $f$ is defined recursively by $f(1)=f(2)=1$ and $$f(n)=f(n-1)-f(n-2)+n$$ for all integers $n\geq 3$. What is $f(2018)$?

steps.title: Where to start: look for a repeating pattern
steps.body: Nobody can compute $2018$ terms by hand, so we need a shortcut. The recursion has alternating signs, $+f(n-1)-f(n-2)$, and signs like that tend to cancel when you combine a few equations. Compute a few terms first to have something to check against.

steps.title: Add two neighboring equations
steps.body:
Write the rule for $n$ and for $n+1$:
$$f(n+1)=f(n)-f(n-1)+(n+1),\qquad f(n)=f(n-1)-f(n-2)+n.$$
Adding them, $f(n)$ and $f(n-1)$ cancel and leave $f(n+1)=-f(n-2)+2n+1$. So each term is tied to the term three places back, with a minus sign.

your_turn.prompt: Check the new rule with $n=3$: what does it give for $f(4)$?

steps.title: Use it twice: jump six places
steps.body:
With $m=n-2$ the rule reads $f(m+3)=-f(m)+2m+5$. Apply it again three places later: $f(m+6)=-f(m+3)+2m+11$. Substituting the first into the second, the minus signs cancel:
$$f(m+6)=f(m)+6\quad\text{for all } m\ge1.$$

your_turn.prompt: Use the six-step rule to find $f(7)$ and $f(8)$ from $f(1)$ and $f(2)$.
your_turn.answer: $f(7)=f(1)+6=7$ and $f(8)=f(2)+6=7$. Careful: $f(7)=7$ might tempt you to guess $f(n)=n$, but $f(6)=8$ and $f(8)=7$ show that guess is wrong.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body:
Divide by $6$: $2018=2+6\cdot336$. So going from $f(2)$ to $f(2018)$ takes $336$ jumps of six places, each adding $6$:
$$f(2018)=f(2)+6\cdot336=1+2016=2017.$$
The answer is **(B)**.

wrong_choices.C: This comes from guessing $f(n)=n$ after seeing values like $f(7)=7$. The sequence does not follow that pattern: for example $f(6)=8$ and $f(8)=7$.

verification.verifier_notes: Hole found by adversarial verifier, fixed, and re-verified by a fresh verifier.
